articles.title: All About the Money review – confusion and compelling weirdness of wealthy leftwing heir
articles.summary: This profile of James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, who set up a commune in rural Massachusetts and is fighting extradition from Spain, is a brave attempt to package a complex character and story.
body: But when the group decide to protest at Elbit Systems, the Israeli-owned arms manufacturer, its actions slide into “criminal mischief and criminal trespassing”, according to reports. Several Alford members are arrested, including one Paige Belanger; O’Shea’s film cuts back and forth between interviews with Belanger and other communards and Chambers, who has scarpered to Tunisia. Although he pays for Belanger’s defence and covers other costs arising from the action, considerable rancour rises between Fergie, Paige and other former Alford community members, that O’Shea perhaps wisely doesn’t let the film get too bogged down with trying to parse.

articles.title: ‘Vicarious wish-fulfillment’: why That Thing You Do! is my feelgood movie
articles.summary: The latest in our ongoing series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films is a journey back to the 90s for Tom Hanks’ heartfelt 60s-set music comedy. “How did we get here?” That’s the question Steve Zahn’s character in That Thing You Do!
body: It’s a moment I have thought of many times over the past 30 years. Sometimes, it’s been a moment I’ve aspired to, and sometimes it’s a moment I’ve felt myself. When the band hears their song on the radio for the first time, it’s one of the most ebullient moments I’ve ever seen on film. There is a euphoria that is recognizable for anyone who has ever felt the joy of a creative accomplishment – and isn’t that all of us, in one way or another? That’s what makes That Thing You Do! my feelgood movie.

In 1996, Tom Hanks was on top of Hollywood. He had back-to-back best actor Oscar wins, and two of 1995’s highest-grossing films with Toy Story and Apollo 13. I presume he could have done anything he wanted. I will be forever grateful that he chose to write, direct and co-star in this modest, gentle ode to 1960s pop music. It’s a movie of such warmth that any scene viewed at any time will instantly make me happier.

articles.title: Ever Since I Knew Myself review – confronting the scars of childhood
articles.summary: Maka Gogaladze’s debut feature looks at generational differences in the context of Georgia’s education system and emphasis on collectivism. The scars imprinted on impressionable young minds can never fully fade away.
body: This debut feature would appear, at first glance, to be another act of revolt. Putting her mother in front of the camera, Gogaladze asks probing, at times blunt, questions about the strict education thrust on her in childhood. Together, they talk about piano lessons that ended in tears, and tough academic exams that continued to haunt the director well into her adulthood. Their contrasting personalities are fascinatingly revealed across these conversations in all their tension, yet these sequences also represent a moving effort to reach across generational differences.

Gogaladze widens the frame to include a series of observational vignettes shot at various children’s classes in Georgia. The subjects vary – history lessons are sandwiched between ballet and dance sessions – yet the disciplined atmosphere remains the same. Even during art class, teachers leave little room for individual expression or debate. Obedience, rather than dialogue, is the order of the day.

articles.title: ‘Nothing worked for me until I was clean and sober’: Ashley Walters on acting, directing – and turning his life around
articles.summary: In Adolescence he proved himself one of the UK’s best actors. Now he has directed his first film, Animol. He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring success. Ashley Walters seems to have lived his life on fast-forward.
body: Back in the early 2000s, he fit a certain stereotype of Black British youth as Asher D, the rapper from deprived and supposedly crime-ridden Peckham, who rolled with the street-tough So Solid Crew, got into beefs with east London rivals such as Dizzee Rascal, was demonised by the tabloids and called a “boasting macho idiot rapper ” by the then culture minister Kim Howells.

So Solid Crew were trailblazing in terms of British hip-hop, but Walters’ view of those times is far from rose-tinted. “Everything other than the music, it was bad, it was negative,” he says. “The music was very British, but if you looked at our style, our clothes, the jewellery, the cars, that was all the Americanised stuff that we wanted to bring into it.” That also included guns – even if, in Walters’ case, the firearm was a modified air pistol.

Asher D was never really him, he says. “Behind the scenes, in all honesty, I was questioning if I was doing the right thing. Because a lot of our success was underpinned with street stuff: you can’t go to that area because you might get shot; you can’t do this because that person has had beef with this person; and it was, like, all this politics.”

He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring success.
Ashley Walters seems to have lived his life on fast-forward.

articles.title: ‘VelociPastor 2’ Leaves FilmQuest Audience Roaring, Celebrating Human-Made Films in an AI Era
articles.summary: Who knew that one of this year’s giddiest celebrations of filmmaking would be a movie where the stunt dummies are obvious, the dinosaur costumes are obviously homemade and you can literally see the strings on special effects shots?
body: The Sunday FilmQuest screening of “VelociPastor 2,” a festival known for attracting audiences filled with indie filmmakers, was primed to enjoy the movie and laughed boisterously throughout. Beyond the jabs at the joys and flaws of low-budget filmmaking, the movie is filled with plenty of other jokes in the spirit of “Airplane!” that kept spirits high.

There was also a sense of gratitude that so many of the jokes showed affection for the “let’s put on a show” enthusiasm that inspires both films. A frequent topic of discussion at the Provo, Utah-based festival has been the infiltration of AI in the industry, which is met with near-universal distrust and disinterest. In fact, one of the biggest applause points before every screening at the fest is a promise that the feature presentation doesn’t include AI.

But the joy of “VelociPastor 2” is the knowing silliness of low-budget filmmaking gone wrong, something that would be too complex to try to craft an AI prompt. Whether it’s miniatures that don’t show the true scope of Italian city life or two extras playing a ferocious game of Frisbee without actually tossing a disc, it feels like a uniquely human satire.

articles.title: Tokyo Film Festival to Reassess Its Global Standing Ahead of 40th Edition, Says Director Hisamatsu Takeo
articles.summary: The Tokyo International Film Festival will review its 39th edition once it wraps and reassess where it stands on the international circuit before its 40th anniversary next year, festival director Hisamatsu Takeo says.
body: “We are somehow in a competitive relationship with the Busan IFF, we’re close geographically and our dates are close too. I think the time has come to re-examine where TIFF should position itself, both within Asia and within the world,” Hisamatsu says.
The appeal of festivals such as Cannes and Venice is bound up with their host cities, he adds.

“Tokyo has a distinctive appeal of its own: it’s a vibrant, multifaceted city where tradition and modernity coexist, and mainstream culture intersects with subculture. These are qualities we should do more to showcase to the world,” he says.

The festival is organized by UniJapan, which also runs the TIFFCOM market and a set of international promotion and support programs. Hisamatsu, who is also UniJapan’s executive director, wants those three arms working more closely together and offering more to filmmakers and producers.

articles.title: Star Flops and Slowing Investment Help Explain China’s Thin Festival Presence, Says Tokyo Programming Director
articles.summary: Star-driven flops at the Chinese box office, slowing investment and a reportedly more complicated censorship process have a bearing on China’s low profile at international festivals this year, according to Ichiyama Shozo, programming director of the Tokyo International Film Festival.
body: Ichiyama has worked closely with Chinese-language auteurs including Hou Hsiao-hsien and Jia Zhangke, and says the mainland industry changed sharply in the mid-2000s. As the economy boomed, multiplexes multiplied and box office prospects rose, even independent projects with no stars attached could raise reasonable budgets in China.
Taiwan, by contrast, looks comparatively steady. Its home market has always been small, Ichiyama says, but a range of public support mechanisms keeps production going.

This year’s lineup is marked by films about historical events, wars among them, Ichiyama says. They include Samuele Rossi’s Competition entry “Even If Hell Came,” which follows a young Italian partisan holding out in the Alps in the winter of 1944.
“I believe this reflects a global trend, as symbolized by the films dealing with the Second World War that were screened at this year’s Cannes Film Festival,” he says.

articles.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
articles.summary: Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme.
body: Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.
A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram, external said he had died "suddenly".
Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.
In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.

articles.title: Spotify uploads lyrics for Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene in Irish
articles.summary: The single is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.
body: The lyrics to Dolly Parton's Welsh version of her hit Jolene were uploaded mistakenly to Spotify in Irish.
The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.
The version has parts of the song sung in English and Welsh - but the lyrics presented on the digital audio streaming service Spotify actually showed the language as Irish.
Spotify removed the Irish lyrics after the BBC approached it for comment.

articles.title: ‘All About the Money’ Doc Maker Explains How She Updated Her Film on Fergie Chambers After His Arrest – and Her Concerns About That U.S. Extradition Request
articles.summary: Irish director Sinéad O’Shea is gearing up for much debate as the film comes into U.K. and Irish cinemas on Oct. 30 after its BFI London Film Festival run and before screening at DOC NYC in November.
body: The works of Irish documentary director Sinéad O’Shea tend to turn heads and cause debate. Her latest film, All About the Money, which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival before recently screening at the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF), is no different.

The film also goes into his pro-Palestine and anti-Israel activism, which has landed him in the headlines in recent months. In July, Spanish authorities arrested Chambers; he is being held in Madrid. The Guardian then reported that FBI agents raided his Ibiza, Spain, vacation rental. The U.S. has made an extradition request, citing Chambers’ alleged financial support of Hamas and other charges.

O’Shea, who wrote and directed the doc, produced by Claire McCabe, Harry Vaughn, Katie Holly, and Sigrid Dyekjær, with SOS Productions and Real Lava co-producing, caught up with THR about the recent activity surrounding the man at the center of her doc, which will screen in U.K. and Ireland cinemas from Oct. 30 after a recent run at the BFI London Film Festival (LFF).
